memoryText: And your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Today there is no new reading. Today is for review and Sabbath rest. This is a combined day, so take it slowly. Rest first, then remember.

Begin with the anchor verse of Unit 9, printed above. Read it aloud several times. Say it from memory if you can. This promise holds together everything you have read in the last sixty-seven days: the anointing of David, the covenant with his house, his sin and his repentance, the glory of Solomon’s temple, and the sad division at the end. The throne is established forever. That is God’s promise, and he does not break his promises.

Notice the sweep of what you have read. A barren woman prays, and a prophet is born. A people ask for a king and get Saul, who fails. God chooses a shepherd boy, who defeats a giant and flees through the wilderness. The throne comes to him, and with it a covenant that outlasts him. He falls, and he is forgiven. His son builds the temple and then loses his heart. The story ends in compromise, but the promise remains.

Read the verse once more, and think of Jesus. Gabriel said to Mary, “The Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever” (Luke 1:32-33). The promise stands because of him. He is the offspring who is also the Son of God, the king who does not fail.

Then rest. Do not catch up on missed readings. Do not do extra work. Take the Sabbath as a gift, a sign that the work of salvation does not depend on you.
unitRecap:
In Unit 9 you have followed the story of the Davidic covenant through 1 and 2 Samuel, 1 Kings 1 to 11, and a large selection of the Psalms. The books of Samuel began with Hannah’s song and ended with David’s altar. In between, you saw Israel ask for a king and receive Saul, whose partial obedience cost him the throne. You saw God choose David, a shepherd, whom he looked at by the heart and not by the appearance.

You saw David as a fugitive: spared Saul twice, learned to strengthen himself in the LORD, and wrote some of the Bible’s greatest prayers in caves and deserts. You saw him become king, take Jerusalem, and bring the ark to the city. And you read the center of the unit, 2 Samuel 7, where God promised David a house, a kingdom, and a throne forever.

You also saw his fall. The affair with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah were followed by Nathan’s confrontation and David’s confession. You read Psalms 32 and 51, the great songs of forgiveness. And you saw the consequences: the violence in his house, Absalom’s rebellion, and David’s weeping flight. God did not abandon the king, and he did not hide the cost of sin.

Solomon’s reign was the high point: wisdom, peace, and the temple. But the narrator also showed the quiet compromises that led to his fall. The kingdom would be torn in two, and yet, for David’s sake, a lamp would remain in Jerusalem.

The Psalms in this unit were the voice of the king and of the people. Psalm 2 showed the anointed Son. Psalms 3 to 5, 13, 18, 22, 24, 32, 34, 51, and 63 gave words for fear, longing, repentance, and trust. Psalms 45 and 72 pointed to the king whose throne is forever and whose rule reaches to the ends of the earth. The theme throughout was that David’s greater Son would come, and that God would keep his word.
weekInReview: This final week of the unit followed the story from the end of David to the beginning of the end of Solomon. You read David’s last words, in which he trusted the everlasting covenant, and the account of the census and plague that ended at the temple mount. You saw Solomon anointed, ask for wisdom, and build the temple, and you read his great prayer at its dedication. In the Psalms you read the royal wedding song of Psalm 45 and the prayer for the king in Psalm 72, and the songs of Zion in Psalms 48, 84, and 87, and David’s vow of integrity in Psalm 101. You ended with Solomon’s fall, and God’s decision to tear the kingdom, but for David’s sake. The week taught that God’s presence is the glory of his people, that his promises stand in spite of human failure, and that we need a greater king.

reviewQuestions.question: What is the covenant God makes with David in 2 Samuel 7?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Recall the promises: a great name, a place for Israel, a son who will build the temple, and a throne established forever. God says he will be a father to the king and discipline him, but his steadfast love will not depart. Notice that David wanted to build God a house, and God said he would build David a house. Write a few sentences about what this covenant promises and why it matters for the rest of the Bible. How does Jesus fulfill it? Look at Luke 1:32-33 and Acts 2:29-36.

reviewQuestions.question: How does David’s sin with Bathsheba illustrate both grace and consequence?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Look back at 2 Samuel 11 and 12 and Psalms 32 and 51. David’s sin was serious, and God sent Nathan to confront him. When David confessed, Nathan said, “The LORD has put away your sin.” Yet the child died and the sword did not leave his house. Write about how forgiveness and consequence can both be true. Where do you see this pattern in your own life? How does the cross hold both justice and mercy together?

reviewQuestions.question: What makes Solomon’s reign both the high point and the beginning of the end?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Think about the wisdom, the peace, the temple, and the prayer of dedication, and then about the horses, the wives, and the high places. The Deuteronomy 17 warnings were ignored one by one. Write a few sentences about how great gifts can lead to great failures. What does Solomon’s story teach about the need for an undivided heart? How does Jesus succeed where Solomon failed?

reviewQuestions.question: What do the Messianic Psalms teach us about the kind of king God ultimately promises?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Look back at Psalms 2, 22, 45, and 72. The king is God’s Son, he suffers and is abandoned, he is addressed as God with an eternal throne, and he defends the poor and rules to the ends of the earth. Write a few sentences describing the king these psalms portray. Which of these features surprises you most? How do they come together in Jesus?

prayerPrompts: Thank God for keeping covenant with David and fulfilling it in Jesus.
Confess where your heart has been divided.
Rest and ask him to keep the unit verse before you.
